claims.claim: OpenStax's Principles of Management defines ethics as involving how we act, live, lead our lives, and treat others — our choices, decision-making processes, and the moral principles and values that govern our behaviors regarding what is right and wrong — and defines business ethics as applied ethics that focuses on real-world situations, asking how we should apply our values to the way we conduct business.

Ethical principles generally are codified into laws and regulations when there is societal consensus about such wrongdoing; following the law (compliance) is therefore narrower than ethics, and the law is a floor rather than a ceiling for right conduct.

Some business practices sit in grey areas that are not illegal but are ethically questionable (for example, a supplier's negotiator hosted in a top hotel suite, close to but not quite bribery), so an action can be legal yet still ethically questionable.

An ethical dilemma is a situation or predicament in which there is not an optimal or desired choice to be made between two options, neither of which solves an issue or delivers an opportunity that is ethical; dilemmas often originate from not sorting out and thinking through potential consequences.

Ethics matters for trust: even small companies increasingly put more emphasis on ethics to restore trust among their customers and the community, and an Ethics & Compliance Initiative survey found 22 percent of global workers report pressure to compromise their standards.

Ethics matters for reputation and long-run survival: poor business ethics can create a very negative image for a company, be expensive for the firm and/or the executives involved, and can result in bankruptcy and jail time for the offenders; organizations reduce these outcomes by educating employees about ethical standards and by leading through example.

The Markkula Center for Applied Ethics' framework for ethical decision making includes a test step that asks: if I told someone I respect (or a public audience) which option I have chosen, what would they say? — the source of the lesson's publicity test.

In organizations, an individual's ethical stance is affected by peers, subordinates, and supervisors as well as by the organizational culture, which can support and encourage ethical actions or promote unethical behavior; employees also follow the examples their leaders set.

Ethics is a set of moral standards for judging whether something is right or wrong, and an ethical issue is a situation where someone must choose between a set of actions that may be ethical or unethical.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the law is a reliable guide to what is ethical
positions: OpenStax's Principles of Management notes that ethical principles are generally codified into laws when society reaches consensus, implying law and ethics overlap heavily
CFI notes grey-area practices that are not illegal but ethically questionable, and the Markkula Center states ethics is not the same as following the law
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the law as a floor, not a ceiling: legality is necessary but not sufficient for rightness. The ethics-versus-compliance section, Question 2, and the Rafael worked example all show legal-but-questionable decisions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether an ethical dilemma always involves two wrong options or can involve two goods in tension
positions: OpenStax's Principles of Management frames dilemmas as two options neither of which is ethical
Common textbook and lay usage also includes two-goods conflicts, where both options are defensible but incompatible
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the wider framing — two goods or two wrongs in tension — with OpenStax's no-clearly-ethical-option definition as the core; the Tessa-and-Omar overtime example is the two-goods case and Question 3 teaches the tension.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 2.1: Understanding Business Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; id reused from the phase-2 registry with identical URL). Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: ethics as a set of moral standards for judging whether something is right or wrong; an ethical issue as a situation where someone must choose between actions that may be ethical or unethical; recognizable categories of unethical business activities (taking things that do not belong to you; saying things you know are not true; giving or allowing false impressions). sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; id reused from the phase-2 registry with identical URL). Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: poor business ethics can create a very negative image for a company, be expensive for the firm and/or the executives involved, and result in bankruptcy and jail time; organizations reduce such outcomes by educating employees about ethical standards, by leading through example, and through ethics training; people are influenced by the ethical environment their employers create; the self-test sequence (legal restrictions, code of ethics, guidelines) as supporting context for the decision-test section. sourceRecords.provider: Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (university ethics center; id reused from the phase-2 registry with identical URL). Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports the publicity test: the framework's 'Choose an Option for Action and Test It' step asks 'If I told someone I respect (or a public audience) which option I have chosen, what would they say?' The lesson's five philosophical lenses are out of scope (philosophy subject owns ethical theory depth); the publicity test is the only framework element taught.
